query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.mechanism: The introduction of dual heterogeneous structures leads to enhanced strength-ductility synergy, as the soft phase provides ductility while the hard phase provides strength. The dual-phase microstructure also hinders grain boundary sliding and dislocation movement during high-temperature deformation, resulting in improved high-temperature strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved strength and room-temperature tensile ductility, with a potential increase in yield strength and tensile strength of up to 20-30% and an improvement in ductility of up to 10-20%.
generation.baseline: Conventional processing methods and previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies
generation.boundary: The introduction of dual heterogeneous structures should be done in a way that maintains the stability of the high-temperature precipitate phase and avoids the formation of brittle phases.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the improvement in strength and ductility is uncertain and may depend on the specific alloy composition and processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Tensile testing of eutectic high-entropy alloys with and without dual heterogeneous structures at room temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the introduction of dual heterogeneous structures does not result in a significant improvement in strength and ductility, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Developing alloys with ultrahigh strength and excellent ductility simultaneously over a wide temperature range is crucial for developing high-temperature steam turbines [,,]. Recently, as a category of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), dual-phase high-entropy alloys (DP-HEAs) with a soft FCC phase and hard BCC (B2) phase have been reported to have excellent strength–ductility synergy at ambient temperature and high temperature [,,,,,,,,,], and thus have great potential to be used as steam turbine hot end components. Unfortunately, due to the rapid softening of the phase with the BCC structure at high temperatures, the yield strength of the alloy will significantly decrease [,,,,,]. Moreover, due to the weakness of grain boundaries and phase boundaries, the cracks initiate rapidly and propagate along the interface during high-temperature deformation, severely limiting the high-temperature application of FCC/B2 dual-phase high-entropy alloys [,,,,].

Multiphase alloys with heterogeneous microstructures demonstrate excellent combination of strength and ductility, making them attractive for myriad structural applications [,,]. Recently, eutectic high entropy alloys (HEAs) with multiple solid solution phases have been the subject of extensive research due to their promise of overcoming the strength-ductility tradeoff seen in metals and conventional alloys [,,,,,,,]. The AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy represents a canonical example of an eutectic HEA with the lamellar arrangement of CoCrFe-rich L12 and AlNi-rich B2 phases [], which exhibit an excellent combination of strength and ductility at room temperature as well as exceptional strain hardening behavior that is largely retained up to 700 °C. Different processing routes have been utilized for achieving a wide range of microstructural features, resulting in outstanding mechanical properties and excellent corrosion resistance in these alloys. The ease of attaining ultrafine microstructure in directly cast eutectic HEAs is uncommon in conventional alloys []. AbstractA lamellar (L12 + B2) AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA) was severely deformed by a novel hybrid-rolling process. During hybrid-rolling, the deformation was carried out in two stages, namely cryo-rolling followed by warm-rolling at 600 °C. The strain (ε) imparted in each of these steps was identical ~1.2, resulting in a total strain of ε~2.4 (corresponding to 90% reduction in thickness). The novel processing strategy resulted in an extremely heterogeneous microstructure consisting of retained lamellar and transformed nanocrystalline regions. Each of these regions consisted of different phases having different crystal structures and chemical compositions. The novel structure-composition dual heterogeneous microstructure originated from the stored energy of the cryo-rolling which accelerated transformations during subsequent low temperature warm-rolling. The dual heterogeneous microstructure yielded an unprecedented combination of strength (~2000 MPa) and ductility (~8%). The present study for the first time demonstrated that dual structure-composition heterogeneities can be a novel microstructural design strategy for achieving outstanding strength-ductility com

Microstructural modifications of HEAs based on mechanical processing, thermomechanical processing and elemental additions have been explored in order to obtain better combinations of mechanical properties. Severe plastic deformation of the CoCrFeMnNi FCC HEA through high pressure torsion was found to result in a large increase in both hardness (520 HV) and strength (1950 MPa), but the development of nano-crystalline microstructure (~ 50 nm) made the alloy brittle. Introduction of twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP) and transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) to the CoCrFeMnNi HEA was found to impart good strain-hardening ability, resulting in a large tensile ductility, albeit at the cost of low values of true ultimate tensile strength (1124 MPa). The use of shot peening to develop a hierarchical microstructure (consisting of a thin deformed layer and an un-deformed core) in a CoCrFeMnNi HEA resulted in a strength increase, but the improvement was limited to only around 700 MPa. decision.trend: The trend in the research on eutectic high-entropy alloys is to improve their strength and ductility by modifying their microstructure through various processing techniques such as cryo-rolling, annealing, and thermomechanical treatment. The research has shown that the introduction of dual heterogeneous structures, nano-lamellar microstructures, and ultrafine-grained duplex microstructures can lead to enhanced strength-ductility synergy. Additionally, the use of alloying additions and control of the c/a ratio in hexagonal close-packed epsilon martensite phase have been explored to improve the mechanical properties of these alloys.
decision.unsolved: The unsolved problem in the research on eutectic high-entropy alloys is to achieve a simultaneous improvement in both strength and ductility, as conventional processing methods often raise strength at the expense of ductility. The room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility of these alloys remain a challenge to be addressed.
decision.why: The introduction of dual heterogeneous structures has been shown to lead to enhanced strength-ductility synergy in eutectic high-entropy alloys. This approach has the potential to address the unsolved problem of achieving a simultaneous improvement in both strength and ductility, and is a plausible next step in the research on these alloys.
